label: Place
name: Samoa
summary:
Samoa, officially the Independent State of Samoa (formerly Western Samoa), is a Polynesian island nation in the South Pacific Ocean. With 220,000 people on two main islands (Upolu and Savai'i), Samoa is one of the South Pacific's oldest independent states and a culturally significant center of Polynesian civilization. Not to be confused with American Samoa (a US territory to the east), Samoa became independent from New Zealand administration in 1962 — the first Pacific Island nation to achieve independence in the 20th century.

Samoan oral tradition traces continuous settlement to over 3,000 years ago, making the Samoan archipelago one of the oldest continuously inhabited Polynesian territories and a significant point in the Polynesian expansion across the Pacific. The fa'asamoa (Samoan way) — a complex social system built on family (aiga), village (nu'u), and the chiefly title system (matai) — has provided remarkable cultural continuity through colonial disruption. Margaret Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) made the islands internationally famous in anthropological discourse, though her conclusions were later controversially challenged by Derek Freeman.

German colonial rule (1900–1914) and New Zealand administration (1914–1962) shaped modern Samoa. The 1918 influenza epidemic, which New Zealand mishandled catastrophically, killed approximately 22% of Samoa's population in one of the Pacific's worst demographic disasters. Independence in 1962 was followed by over six decades of political stability under the dominant Human Rights Protection Party — and Samoa shifted its International Date Line position in 2011 to align economically with Australia and New Zealand.

The country's achievement of independence from New Zealand administration in 1962 marked a milestone for Pacific Island nations seeking self-governance.
